source_title: Diljit's Delhi tickets remained unsold just hours before concert. Is he too pricey for his fans? - India Today
source_excerpt:
Diljit Dosanjh has taken Punjabi music from local gatherings in Punjab to Coachella and Madison Square Garden. He sold out London's Wembley. So, why did tickets for the Delhi concert remain unsold till the last moment?
Delhi is hosting one of India's biggest music stars today. But hours before Diljit Dosanjh takes the stage at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium , there was an unusual sight for an artiste of his stature. Tickets were still up for grabs. Although BookMyShow now lists Diljit Dosanjh's Delhi concert as sold out, tickets were still available at 12 pm, barely four hours before the show.
Unofficial WhatsApp groups, meanwhile, were buzzing with a different kind of activity — fans looking to offload their tickets, at prices lower than what they had paid. The demand and supply in these groups, it appears, are not quite matching up.
For a singer who has packed stadiums across the world, made history at Coachella, performed sold-out shows at Madison Square Garden (New York), Wembley Stadium (London), and appeared on American late-night TV time and again, this is an interesting moment. International stars often see tickets disappear within minutes of booking windows opening. Diljit, too, has enjoyed that kind of frenzy. His previous India tour, Dil-Luminati, was a massive commercial success, with shows selling out rapidly.
So what explains the apparent hesitation in Delhi ?
It might have less to do with Diljit Dosanjh 's popularity and more to do with the price of watching him perform, and a fatigue factor.
According to Ticketmaster, one of the world's largest ticketing platforms and a major provider of ticketing services for live entertainment events, the artiste's team sets the face-value price of concert tickets. It says the artiste plans a tour in consultation with their manager, agent and promoter, with the group jointly deciding the venues, ticket-sale dates and distribution channels, including pre-sales.
Ticketmaster also says artistes and their teams retain the bulk of ticket-sale revenues, often 100 per cent of the face value, while venues and ticketing providers generally do not receive a share of the ticket revenue.
Concert-going has become an increasingly expensive proposition in India, particularly for large-format shows featuring international and homegrown stars. Diljit's Delhi concert is no exception. While the cheapest ticket categories were initially listed at Rs 1,999 and Rs 2,499, the lower-priced inventory was sold out within a few hours.
The cheapest tickets available to buyers at 12 pm on Friday were priced at Rs 6,499, including taxes. At the other end of the spectrum, Fanpit tickets cost Rs 14,999, making it a considerable outlay even for fans who have followed him for years.
But the cost of attending a concert does not end with just the ticket. Once inside the venue, spending keeps adding up. At events such as Lollapalooza Mumbai, for instance, concertgoers have to recharge their QR codes even to buy a bottle of water. And for those looking to enjoy a drink, a pint of beer can cost upwards of Rs 800-900.
For students and young professionals who are just starting their careers and are often on relatively modest incomes, these expenses can be a deterrent. A group of four could end up spending well over Rs 20,000 just on entry, before factoring in food, drinks and other incidentals. Getting to and from the venue can add to the bill, too, with ride-hailing apps often charging three to four times their usual fares during peak concert hours.
Gurpreet Hundal, a longtime Diljit fan who has followed the singer since his early days, told India Today Digital, "The crowd at his concerts is largely young, mostly in the 20s and 30s. There are curious listeners from older age groups too, but a sizeable chunk comprises college students, particularly in cities like Mumbai and Delhi."
Delhi has a sizeable Punjabi population and a large urban youth audience that forms a natural constituency for Diljit's music. His songs, language, humour and cultural references have a direct connection with the city. Today, he is a homegrown star performing for people among whom his music has long been popular. advertisement A STAR WHOSE MUSIC HAS A MUCH BIGGER ECONOMY Union Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat has recently spoken about the economic potential of Diljit Dosanjh's concerts, putting their contribution to the economy at around Rs 500 crore. An Ernst & Young (EY) report released in March 2026 estimated that Diljit's 2024 Dil-Luminati India Tour generated a socio-economic impact of Rs 943 crore. The tour covered 13 cities through 14 performances, attracted more than 3.2 lakh attendees and generated employment across the live-events ecosystem. Nearly 38% of attendees travelled from other cities to attend the concerts. There is, therefore, a strong case for large concerts to be commercially viable. Global-standard production, stadium infrastructure, logistics, security, artists and crew all come at a cost. Nor should an Indian artiste be expected to charge less simply because he or she performs in India. Diljit has earned his place among the biggest names in global music, and his shows are a premium entertainment experience. But the question is whether premium pricing should come at the expense of accessibility, particularly when the artiste has such a deep connection with his home audience. advertisement FROM PUNJAB'S ORCHESTRAS TO THE WORLD'S BIGGEST STAGES Diljit's journey makes the question of his ticket prices particularly relevant. He did not emerge from the machinery of a global record label or a metropolitan music industry. He began by singing devotional songs and performing at local gatherings in Punjab, releasing his first album as a teenager. From those early years on the Punjabi music circuit, he went on to become one of the most recognisable Indian artistes internationally. Today, he sells out global venues, takes Punjabi music to audiences who might not understand the language, and carries the culture of Punjab onto global stages. Yet, much of his appeal at home comes from the fact that he has not shed the desi personality that made people warm to him. His Instagram Reels, spontaneous humour and easy-going public persona have helped him remain relatable even as his celebrity has grown. And it is worth asking whether fans who helped build that connection should have to think twice before spending a sizeable portion of their monthly income to see him live. This is not an argument that Diljit should perform cheaply, or that a global star should not command premium prices. It is about having enough room in the pricing structure for the fans who cannot afford a luxury concert experience. advertisement However, fan fatigue could be a reason for the availability of tickets till the very last moment of Diljit's Delhi concert. Some fans may have already watched Diljit perform during his Dil-Luminati India Tour barely two years ago and may not be keen to spend again so soon. The Ahmedabad show was also announced first, prompting many fans to try booking tickets there before turning to Delhi. "When Diljit's Ahmedabad show was announced, there was no mention that he would be doing a multi-city tour. Many fans from Delhi ended up booking tickets for Ahmedabad, only for the Delhi show to be announced later as a surprise. This left many annoyed as well," said a Diljit fan. Add to this the growing number of concerts competing for the same young audience, and fans may simply be becoming more selective about which shows they spend on. For an artiste who has travelled from the grassroots of Punjab to Coachella and Madison Square Garden, performing in Delhi is also a homecoming. - Ends
